label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Dear Jonno, re: the coolroom (since you won't stop asking)**

Righto Jonno. You've messaged me about six times since you saw my story so here it is, the whole thing, in writing, so I never have to explain it again. Everyone else reading this (hi mum), this one's basically a letter to Jonno, sorry. You can stay though.

So. Cup Day.

I rock up at 6.40am on Tuesday the 3rd, nice and early, feeling like a responsible adult. Open the coolroom to start pulling stuff for prep and something's off. You know when you walk into a coolroom and it hugs you with that cold? Didn't happen. It was just a room. A small, damp, slightly sad room. Look at the thermometer and it's sitting on 11 degrees.

Eleven, Jonno.

The compressor had carked it sometime overnight Monday into Tuesday and just sat there in the dark letting everything warm up like it was on holiday. Which, on Cup Day, with 140 covers booked for lunch, set menu, three courses, is honestly a hate crime.

And Raff was off that day. So guess who was running the show. Yours truly. Me. The guy you once watched burn a whole tray of garlic bread because he was arguing with you about whether a hot dog is a sandwich (it is, still, I'll die on this hill).

First thing I did was ring Phil. I want you to really picture this. I tell him the coolroom's dead, it's 11 degrees, we've got 140 people coming, and he goes, and I quote, "just make it work mate."

Just make it work mate.

Phil, that is not a plan. That's a vibe. You can't put "just make it work mate" in a fridge.

Then I rang Wally from Coldline, love Wally, and Wally says he can't come till Wednesday because the part has to come down from Sydney. So the part's having a nicer week than me, cool cool cool.

So we did what every bistro kitchen in the history of the world has done in a crisis, which is panic quietly and start shoving things into whatever's cold. Both undercounters got packed like a Tetris game on level 40. The bar fridge got commandeered, so the beers got evicted, and yes, there was some grief from front of house about that, and no, I didn't care. Then I went next door to Marta's cafe with my best sad puppy face and she let us have half her walk-in.

Which brings me to the beef.

We had 30kg of beef shin that needed to go next door. 30 kilos. So me and Benny load it onto the old milk crate trolley, the one with the dodgy wheel you always said was going to kill someone, and head off down the laneway. It's raining, obviously, because the universe had decided I was the main character that day. About halfway down, the dodgy wheel just leaves. Pops off and rolls away like it's got somewhere better to be. So now it's me and Benny in the rain, holding up a three-wheeled trolley full of beef, sort of dragging and sort of carrying it, swearing at each other the whole way. Benny's got rain in his eyes and he keeps saying "lift with your legs" like he's my physio. Mate I'm lifting with everything I've got.

Meanwhile Kev, legend, absolute king of the dish pit, gets sent to the servo for ice. He comes back with 14 bags and fills up the old esky. The servo guy apparently looked at him with 14 bags of ice at 7.30 on a Tuesday morning and asked if we were having a party. Kev said "yeah mate, a big one" and just walked out. Didn't explain. I love him.

So all up, we lost about 1800 bucks of stock. Mostly dairy, which was never going to survive, and the duck legs, which I'm still grieving honestly. Those duck legs did nothing wrong. RIP.

Then service.

Here's the thing Jonno, and I need you to really take this in. You would have lost your absolute mind. London's made you soft. I've seen your Instagram, you're having flat whites in places with exposed brick and a dog in the window. You've gone soft. Old Jonno would've been yelling at the coolroom. New Jonno would have cried. Probably into a little oat milk something.

Anyway. 12.15 we're mid-service and I realise the panna cotta's not happening. They'd been in the coolroom, they'd gone soft and sad and slightly wrong, so I 86'd them. Dessert became "affogato with whatever." Whatever being whatever we had left. Bit of ice cream, shot of coffee, some crumbled biscuit, a bit of toffee shard on a couple. Just making it up.

And people LOVED it. Like more than they would've loved the panna cotta. I had a table ask if it was going on the regular menu. It's not a dish mate, it's a cry for help. But sure.

Best moment of the day though, for me, was the lady on table 9. Turns out table 9 has a straight view out the side window onto the laneway. So she's watched me and Benny haul a mountain of beef through the rain on a broken trolley like two blokes moving a body. And when her main comes out she asks the waiter, very politely, if the beef was "free range from the laneway."

Free range from the laneway. I think about it every day now. I want it on a shirt.

Now Marta, being a businesswoman, has decided we owe her for the walk-in. Not in money. In croissant credit. So the deal is I'm basically doing staff meal for her lot for about three weeks. Every time I see her she just goes "croissant credit" and walks off. It's a good deal for her and I respect it.

Oh and the cherry on top. My horse in the work sweep. The horse I drew, on the day my coolroom died. Was called Ice Cold Lad.

Ice Cold Lad, Jonno.

Came second last. The universe was taking the piss and it wanted me to know.

But here's the bit I actually wanted to tell you, and then I'll stop being soft myself. It was honestly the best service we did all year. Everyone was locked in. Nobody whinged, nobody went missing for a durry at the wrong time, Benny didn't sulk once, which is a first, Kev was running ice and dishes like a machine, front of house were bang on with the dessert change, and we got every one of those 140 covers out. The pass was quiet in that good way where everyone just knows what they're doing. I've been chasing that feeling for months and it turns out all it took was a broken compressor, a three-wheeled trolley and a lot of fear.

I've decided this is my big life lesson: bistro kitchens don't actually run on refrigeration. They run on bar fridges and spite.

Wally came Wednesday, the part had made it down from Sydney, coolroom's back to normal and freezing my hands off again like it should. Phil came in Thursday and said "see, told you it'd work out." Phil. Mate. You didn't do anything. You said a sentence.

Anyway, that's the whole saga. Next time you message me "wait what happened with the coolroom" I'm just sending you this link and nothing else.

Miss having you on grill. Benny's alright but he doesn't sing the wrong words to Khe Sanh like you did, and the hot dog debate's gone stale without you.

Come home ya flog.

— your favourite sous chef
